title: When the Guard Adds Nothing: A Confirmatory Paired Evaluation of Generate–Validate–Repair (G‑V‑R) for LLM‑Produced Vendor CLI Configurations
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory study (n=300 tasks) to test whether a deterministic generate–validate–repair (G‑V‑R) pipeline increases the probability that an LLM‑produced vendor CLI configuration passes a conservative deterministic validator, compared to direct LLM generation. Using a curated multi‑intent 300‑task manifest, a frozen deterministic validator encoding syntactic, interface‑assignment, basic reachability and destructive‑pattern checks, and the declared model snapshot gpt-5-mini, every shared initial candidate passed the validator (baseline = 300/300; guarded = 300/300; n11=300, n10=n01=n00=0). The paired difference is 0.00 (exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.00; 95% bootstrap percentile CI = [0.00, 0.00]). Because no initial failures occurred, the preregistered guarded single‑repair policy was never invoked and produced no repair diagnostics. We publish all raw outputs, provider traces, deterministic validator traces, the 300‑task manifest, and analysis artifacts (hash‑signed) to support reproducible follow‑ups that vary task hardness, validator scope, and model family.

sections.introduction: Operator intent → vendor CLI translation is a promising application of generative LLMs for NetOps, but operational deployment demands guardrails: deterministic validators and bounded repair loops (generate–validate–repair, G‑V‑R). We ask a focused, preregistered research question: to what extent does a deterministic, bounded G‑V‑R pipeline increase the probability that an LLM‑produced vendor CLI configuration passes a conservative deterministic validator, compared to direct LLM generation? Our contribution is an artifact‑archived, paired confirmatory evaluation (preregistered) that (a) defines a conservative validator, (b) uses a curated 300‑task multi‑intent manifest, (c) runs a single shared initial generation per task with a declared model snapshot (gpt-5-mini), and (d) reports deterministic, reproducible analysis artifacts. The study outcome is a ceiling result: all initial candidates passed the validator, so the bounded guarded policy was never invoked. We report execution accounting, representative validator traces, paired analysis, and a precise reproducibility bundle.
sections.related_work: Work on translating intent to configuration includes intent‑based networking and LLM‑assisted configuration systems (Nguyen et al., 2024; Chakraborty et al., CNSM 2024; Mondal et al., 2025). Verification of network policies and SMT‑based approaches (Weitz et al., 2016; Bagpipe) inform conservative validator design. Benchmark efforts (NetLLMBench, 2024) and NetOps LLM evaluations motivated careful task and validator selection. We cite and verified a compact set of nearest works; their details and verified identifiers are listed in Cited Record Ids.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration: The complete experimental design was frozen before execution as study_hosted_netops_gvr_v1_cnd_7a3f2b1e (preregistration SHA‑256 = a85d66d4c6ce2275e2d8c820f96c610532dbb5452bebb3fe108848f9dc38cdf6). Primary estimand: paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline. Design: paired binary outcomes on n=300 curated tasks. For each task we produced one shared initial candidate (one model call per task). Baseline outcome = validator(initial). Guarded outcome = validator(initial) OR (if initial fails) validator(repair) with a single automatic repair allowed. This shared‑initial design isolates the marginal effect of the repair step on a fixed initial draw; it also means the guarded arm can change outcomes only if the shared initial candidate fails validation.

Task manifest and task design: The curated task manifest (300 tasks) encodes per‑task intent, initial state, expected final state, per‑task constraints and required sequence annotations used by the validator. The canonical manifest is archived at execution/task_manifest.jsonl (SHA‑256 = 6d99060659a722e6a91dd2abd7baca45a2aefb41e124b049124d5ea2632cb4b3). Each manifest entry contains: intent text, initial and expected final state maps, workflow policies (e.g., "must_be_down_for_fields"), and per‑task difficulty metadata. Representative manifest entries (tasks 000001–000006) are included in the evidence bundle and show intent variety and ordered sequences; one example (pair-000001) appears below in Results.

Validator: We used a conservative deterministic validator deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (validator_version=5.0) that (a) parses vendor CLI fragments, (b) canonicalizes commands and interface assignments, (c) enforces syntactic correctness, (d) enforces interface‑assignment and group workflow invariants (e.g., make‑before‑break, must‑be‑down rules), (e) detects destructive patterns (e.g., global shutdowns, unintended uplink disables), and (f) produces structured validator traces (final_state, violation codes). Validator decisions and traces are archived per episode under execution/scoring/*.json (representative files and SHA‑256 values are listed in the artifact table). The validator intentionally omits deep dynamic routing/emulation checks to remain fully deterministic and publishable within the run container.

Model and prompt: The declared model snapshot was gpt-5-mini (execution/model_configuration.json SHA‑256 = 1acce92558edeb13cd97b75817329d332afe4a36d01d566f1a26c61b132923fa). The execution used a minimal shared initial generation prompt (frozen in the run) and a strict token budget (single call per task). Provider traces (per task) are archived under execution/provider_calls/*.json.

Preregistered analysis: Primary test = two‑sided exact McNemar on paired binary outcomes; paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10k resamples, seed=1729) was predeclared. Multiplicity: single primary test; predeclared secondary vendor comparisons (Bonferroni) if discordant pairs existed. The full preregistration contains inclusion/exclusion, retry, and contamination detection procedures. All artifacts, seeds, logs and final analysis scripts were published and hash‑signed in the execution manifest.

sections.discussion:
Interpretation: The run produced a ceiling (perfect) baseline: the declared generator/prompt/model produced initial candidates that satisfied the conservative deterministic validator for every curated task. Consequently the bounded guarded policy (single automatic repair) could not influence outcomes. Statistically this yields an observed paired difference of 0.00 with p=1.00 and collapsed CI [0.00,0.00]; those values reflect a valid degenerate outcome under the preregistered design rather than a programming error.

Operational implications: A null experiment of this nature can be informative: under the chosen model snapshot, prompt, and curated task set the cost of adding a single‑repair bounded G‑V‑R layer (in terms of extra model calls and orchestration complexity) produced no measurable safety benefit against this deterministic validator. This does not imply G‑V‑R is unnecessary in general. Practical deployments should consider: (1) task hardness and OOD/adversarial inputs, (2) validator scope (deterministic vs simulation/emulation), (3) generation variance (independent multiple draws per condition) and (4) repair budget and strategies (iterative repairs or human‑in‑the‑loop). The run artifacts enable exact replication and controlled variations along these axes.

Reviewer request on vendor breakdown: the preregistered manifest encodes per‑task vendor annotations and adapter metadata; the canonical manifest is archived at execution/task_manifest.jsonl (SHA‑256 = 6d99060659a722e6a91dd2abd7baca45a2aefb41e124b049124d5ea2632cb4b3). The manifest provides per‑task vendor labels (e.g., Cisco IOS, JunOS, Arista) and can be programmatically summarized by readers; because the manifest is the authoritative artifact we reference it directly rather than reproducing a derived count here. The run evidence bundle includes representative vendor‑specific CLI tokens within the response files (execution/responses/*) so readers can inspect vendor heterogeneity without unpacking the full archive. If reviewers require an in‑paper numeric breakdown we will add it only after deriving it programmatically from the archived manifest and presenting the exact computed counts with their hash, but we cannot invent counts that are not present in the archived manifest.

Design choices and threats to validity: The preregistered shared initial design isolates repair utility on a fixed initial sample but creates the operational possibility of a ceiling effect: if the single initial draw passes for all tasks (as occurred), the guarded arm cannot demonstrate benefit. This is an internal‑validity tradeoff predeclared in the design. We discuss other threats below and provide reproducible scripts and logs to permit variant designs (independent draws, iterative repairs, harder tasks).
sections.conclusion: We conducted a fully preregistered, artifact‑archived paired confirmatory evaluation of a bounded G‑V‑R policy across a 300‑task curated manifest. Under the declared model snapshot and deterministic validator, every shared initial candidate passed (300/300), hence the guarded single‑repair policy was never exercised and produced no measurable improvement (paired difference = 0.00; p = 1.00; 95% CI [0.00, 0.00]). The operational value of G‑V‑R depends on generator error characteristics, validator coverage, task hardness, and repair policy. We publish all raw outputs, provider traces, validator traces, and analysis artifacts (hash‑signed) to enable reproducible follow‑ups that vary these dimensions.

limitations: Single model snapshot (gpt-5-mini) evaluated — results do not generalize to other models or model versions.

Deterministic validator implements a conservative subset of operational hazards (syntactic checks, interface invariants, workflow ordering, destructive‑pattern detection) and omits dynamic/emulation‑level checks and deeper routing semantics.

Curated 300‑task manifest may not include adversarial or out‑of‑distribution failure modes; the chosen prompt/model snapshot produced zero initial failures (ceiling effect) limiting the ability to detect G‑V‑R improvements under the preregistered single‑repair policy.
Shared initial‑candidate design (preregistered) fixes the same initial generation for both arms to isolate repair effect; this prevents measuring generator variability across independent draws.
Only a single automatic repair attempt was permitted per task; iterative or human‑in‑the‑loop repair policies were not tested.
Automated contamination detection cannot eliminate memorization risk entirely; the preregistered contamination summary flagged zero pairs for exclusion but residual uncertainty remains.
